title: Women’s IschemiA TRial to Reduce Events In Non-ObstRuctive CAD (WARRIOR): a randomised controlled trial

sections.abstract:
Women with angina due to suspected ischaemia referred for coronary angiography often have no obstructive coronary artery disease (ANOCA/INOCA).

To determine if intensive medical treatment (IMT) reduces major ischaemic events (major adverse cardiovascular event, MACE) among women with suspected ANOCA/INOCA.

Randomised, prospective, blinded-outcomes evaluation.

71 sites in the USA.

2476 women with suspected ANOCA/INOCA.

IMT-high intensity statin, ACE inhibitor (ACEi) or angiotensin receptor blocker (ARB) and aspirin versus usual care (UC).

Primary: all cause death, myocardial infarction, stroke/transient ischaemic attack, hospitalisation for angina or heart failure (MACE). Secondary: components of the primary, quality of life and win ratio.

Recruitment was lower than planned (n=2476), yielding an aged population (mean, 64 years) with well-controlled blood pressure and low-density lipoprotein cholesterol at baseline, and relatively high rates of statin and ACEI/ARB use. At 2.5 years, 421 events occurred (221 in IMT, 200 in UC) with no difference in the primary outcome (HR=1.13 (95% CI 0.94 to 1.37) for IMT vs UC, p=0.20) or secondary outcomes. Hospitalisations for angina were the dominant contributor to MACE. Sensitivity analysis of contamination provided an estimated HR for IMT versus UC of 0.74 95% CI (0.352 to 1.558), p=0.43.

Among women with suspected ANOCA/INOCA, outcomes were dominated by chest pain and IMT did not improve outcomes, although limited power precludes concluding that it may not be helpful. The findings support the need for more investigation in this population with high burden of angina hospitalisation, health resource consumption and poor quality of life.

NCT03417388 .

Keywords: Angina Pectoris, Women, Microvascular Angina, Chest Pain
sections.introduction:
Cardiovascular (CV) disease, principally ischaemic heart disease (IHD), is the leading cause of death and major contributor to disability for women. 1 Modifiable risk factors (hypertension, diabetes, dyslipidaemia, obesity, overweight and low fitness) are prevalent in these women. 2 Among women with symptoms and/or signs of ischaemia referred for coronary assessment, up to 70% have no obstructive coronary artery disease (CAD); termed ischaemia and no obstructive CAD (angina/ischaemia with no obstructive coronary artery disease (ANOCA/INOCA)). Previously considered ‘low risk’, 3 emerging data document a higher than expected risk for major adverse CV events (MACE, as death, myocardial infarction (MI), stroke/transient ischaemic attack (TIA), or hospitalisation for chest pain or heart failure (HF)) versus case-matched asymptomatic individuals. 4 Coronary endothelial and/or microvascular dysfunction, coronary spasm, diffuse non-obstructive atherosclerosis, have all been implicated, 2 while a recent study has described specific endotypes. 5 Persisting angina, high risk factor burden and stress testing ischaemia identify those at highest risk; however, most risk assessments underestimate risk in these women. 6 Estimates indicate ~4 million patients in the USA (>60% women) have suspected ANOCA/INOCA, incurring healthcare costs similar to those of obstructive CAD. 2

Prior, short-term pilot trials suggested intensive medical therapy (IMT), using high-intensity statins with ACE inhibitors (ACEIs) or angiotensin receptor blockers (ARBs) at maximally tolerated doses, reduced angina, improved stress test results and/or myocardial perfusion with beneficial coronary endothelial and microvascular effects. 7 8 However, larger and longer-term treatment trials have not been performed. Furthermore, Class I treatment guidelines are lacking for ANOCA/INOCA. Current management focuses on symptom control and primary risk factor management (eg, usual care (UC)). Persisting angina symptoms leading to recurrent episodes of primary and secondary care drive up healthcare resource consumption compared with similar asymptomatic individuals. 9

Given the symptom burden, healthcare resource consumption, poor quality of life (QoL) and MACE risk of suspected ANOCA/INOCA, the Women’s IschemiA TRial to Reduce Events In Non-ObstRuctive (WARRIOR) trial was designed as a large, pragmatic MACE outcome trial aimed at testing a strategy supported by pilot pharmacological probe trials conducted in similar heterogeneous cohorts of women and implemented in a fashion and clinical site setting where women were typically seen.
sections.methods:
The WARRIOR CAD trial is a multicentre, prospective, randomised, blinded outcome evaluation design using a pragmatic strategy of providing IMT versus usual UC, planned in 4422 clinically stable women with suspected INOCA due to angina with no obstructive CAD (ANOCA)( NCT 03417388 ). The trial was undertaken in the USA. The protocol has been previously published 10 ( online supplemental figure S1 ).

ANOCA/INOCA was defined as chest pain consistent with angina or equivalent symptoms of sufficient severity to undergo clinically indicated coronary angiography by invasive coronary angiography or coronary CT angiography (CCTA) for suspected IHD but found to have no obstructive CAD. Due to the pragmatic point of care design, sites identified that the participant had symptoms and signs of ischaemia and further documented that they had any of the following: chest pain, abnormal ECG, abnormal stress test, abnormal troponin, shortness of breath and other angina equivalents. Inclusion criteria were ≥18 years old with non-obstructive CAD (as 0 to 49% diameter reduction of a major epicardial vessel or FFR>0.80). Exclusion criteria are detailed 10 and specifically included intolerance to both an ACEI and ARB or statin unless taking a proprotein convertase subtilisin/kexin type 9 (PCSK9) inhibitor. Premenopausal women had negative urine pregnancy tests. Eligible patients signed informed consent.

The primary outcome included time to first occurrence of MACE as all-cause death, non-fatal MI, non-fatal stroke/TIA or hospitalisation for chest pain or HF. Hospitalisation for chest pain was anticipated to be the most frequent MACE given prior registries. 4 Secondary outcomes included: (1) individual components of the primary outcome, (2) QoL using Seattle Angina Questionnaire (SAQ), 11 (3) CV death, (4) time to return to work and (5) healthcare utilisation and cost-effectiveness (the latter two reported subsequently). Outcomes were ascertained at each site, with source documentation adjudicated by the Clinical Events Committee, a group of experts experienced in CV disease including stroke. All-cause death was used in the primary outcome, because CV death may be less classified in non-obstructive CAD and all-cause death is resistant to ascertainment bias.

An integrated web-based, real-time modified REDCap data capture system facilitated recruitment, enrolment, randomisation and outcome collection. Randomisation was 1:1 using SAS V.9.4 (SAS Institute operationalised at sites as detailed in the Supplement. The system included an e-prescription/express mail pharmacy or local pharmacies 12 enabling prescription of IMT medications (atorvastatin or rosuvastatin) and ACEI (lisinopril) (or ARB (losartan)) within 3–4 days. Providing medication at no cost yields superior medication management using structured medication algorithms. 12

The study was initiated on 9 February 2018. There were 71 US sites using web-based, real-time data entry and management. After randomisation, IMT drugs were express mailed or delivered through local pharmacies. Follow-up was at 3, 6 and 12 months and every 6 months thereafter. If adverse events occurred, participants completed a ‘release of medical record’ to accurately record what happened and report de-identified information to the DSMB, CEC, study sponsor and IRBs. Adherence to IMT in both groups was defined by combined use of a high intensity statin, maximally tolerated ACEi or ARB and low dose aspirin. IMT group contamination was defined by a participant not taking an aspirin, and not on maximally tolerated RAS-blockade and not on maximally tolerated statin, while UC group contamination was defined by a participant taking an aspirin and taking a high-intensity RAS-blockade and statin. Monthly reports were sent to sites regarding non-adherence to IMT along with adherence improvement strategies. Monthly PI/coordinator calls were held and adherence strategies were reviewed. The DCC adherence PI contacted PIs and study teams to review non-compliance and review strategies to improve deployment of the IMT strategy.

The COVID-19 pandemic had a major impact on the trial. Initially, recruitment was halted at all sites as there was temporary cessation of all non-essential research activities at most clinical sites. The extended length of the pandemic, crowding of emergency rooms, fear of going to hospital as well as restriction of hospital admissions and semielective procedures like cardiac catheterisation were key factors contributing to reductions in screening and enrolment.

The 14 November 2022 WARRIOR Data Safety Monitoring Board recommendations in response to the pandemic were to ‘continue the trial, maximise recruitment efforts to reach the original goal, if possible, enrol more women with invasive coronary angiography, and focus on collecting biorepository samples on all newly enrolled participants’. Because the DSMB was aware of patient outcomes, an independent review committee, masked to ongoing outcome results, was convened and it further recommended to continue and retain the original primary outcome. When funding was exhausted after 3 no-cost extensions, the study was terminated on 15 February 2025.

The Statistical Analysis Plan is included in the online supplemental file . All major comparisons between randomised groups were according to the ‘intention-to-treat’ (ITT) principle. Women experiencing non-fatal events among the primary or secondary outcomes remained in the trial and in their assigned treatment strategy until closeout.

Statistical comparison with respect to the primary outcome was ‘time-to-event’ analysis based on time from randomisation to first occurrence of any of the following: all-cause death, non-fatal MI, non-fatal stroke/TIA, or hospitalisation for either angina or HF. The trial design estimated effect size of 20% MACE reduction was from randomised controlled trials of statins, low-density lipoprotein cholesterol (LDL-C) reduction and ACEI/ARB blood pressure (BP) reduction. 812 , 14 Planned power considerations used a log-rank test with 80% power at 5% significance level with the following assumptions: drop-out rate of 10%, 3-year MACE rate for the UC arm of 25%, follow-up period of 18 months, enrolment period of 24 months, loss of follow-up of 2% and contamination rates varying from 10% up to 30%, resulting in a planned sample size of 4422 ( online supplemental table S1 ).

Kaplan-Meier curves are presented with log-rank p value. In the primary analysis, Cox proportional hazards regression, stratified by site, was used to calculate HRs and 95% CIs. The analysis was repeated for the following combinations of secondary MACE events (1) composite outcome of CV-death, non-fatal MI or non-fatal stroke/TIA; (2) composite outcome CV-death, non-fatal MI or hospitalisation for chest pain or HF; (3) all-cause mortality; (4) CV-death; (5) total MI (fatal plus non-fatal); (6) resuscitated cardiac arrest; (7) hospitalisation for chest pain; (8) hospitalisation for HF; (9) total stroke/TIA and (10) composite outcome of CV-death, non-fatal MI, stroke/TIA or hospitalisation for chest pain or HF.

Secondary analyses of primary outcome MACE, considering repeated events with the number of previous events as a time-dependent covariate, were performed using the Andersen-Gill model with frailty to describe repeated events. As contamination was anticipated, a sensitivity analysis used inverse probability weighting to reweight participants to minimise post-randomisation confounding. 15 16 Time-varying stabilised weights were calculated as the product between treatment stabilised weights and censoring stabilised weighted over time. Treatment stabilised weights were defined as the ratio between probabilities such that the numerator is the probability of adherence to randomised strategy at a given follow-up month and the denominator is the probability of adherence to randomised strategy at a given follow-up month adjusted by covariates (past IMT fraction on follow-up visits, visit in follow-up, age, and the following baseline values: body mass index, systolic BP (SBP), diastolic BP, heart rate, high-density lipoprotein cholesterol, total cholesterol and SAQ7). Censoring stabilised weights were defined as the ratio between probabilities such that the numerator is the probability of censoring at a given follow-up month and the denominator is the probability of censoring at a given follow-up month adjusted by baseline covariates (same list). These probabilities were estimated based on logistic regression models using the available data at each follow-up month to 5 years.
sections.results:
A total of 2476 women were randomised at 71 sites ( figure 1 ). The first patient was randomised on 9 February 2018 and the last on 18 January 2024. A total of 4% were lost to follow-up, evenly distributed in both arms and included as ITT in the analyses. Pertinent baseline characteristics by treatment assignment are in table 1 and were similar between groups. Participants reflected baseline well-controlled BP, LDL-C, and high rates of statin, ACEI or ARB and aspirin use. Major adverse events are listed in the online supplemental file .

ACEI, ACE inhibitor; ARB, angiotensin receptor blocker; BMI, body mass index; CAD, coronary artery disease; CCTA, coronary CT angiography; LDL-C, low-density lipoprotein cholesterol; SAQ, Seattle Angina Questionnaire; SBP, systolic blood pressure.

The median follow-up for MACE was 3.03 years, ranging from 6 months to 5 years and averaged 2.92 years. There were 421 first events overall (221 in IMT, 200 in UC). The event rate was 17% over 5 years follow-up (17.84% in IMT and 16.17% in UC; p=0.26). A Cox proportional hazards regression (unadjusted), stratified by site was not significantly different between groups (HR=1.13,95% CI 0.94 to 1.37) for IMT versus UC, p=0.20 ( figure 2 ). At 5 years, there were a total of 369 events in the IMT group and 354 in the UC group (frailty model HR 1.01, 95% CI 0.85 to 1.21, p=0.92; table 2 ).

CV, cardiovascular; IMT, intensive medical treatment; MACE, major adverse cardiovascular event; MI, myocardial infarction; TIA, transient ischaemic attack.

Other outcomes appear in table 2 and online supplemental figure S2 . Overall, hospitalisations for angina/chest pain dominated MACE, with fewer non-fatal MI and stroke/TIA. There were four CV deaths in the IMT group and five in the UC group (HR 0.7, 95% CI 0.2 to 2.48), p=0.58; table 2 ). Non-CV and indeterminate deaths are in online supplemental table S2 .

There was no evidence in exploratory analyses of a differential treatment effect on the primary outcome with respect to baseline characteristics, or in prespecified analyses including type of coronary angiography (ICA or CCTA), risk factors, medications, SAQ7, age or site ( online supplemental figure S3 ). A prespecified Cox proportional hazards regression stratified by site for differences in outcome related to CCTA versus ICA did not demonstrate statistical significance for the interaction, p=0.65.

The trial design anticipated contamination (cross-over) in both groups ( online supplemental tables S1 and S2 ). Using suspected ANOCA/INOCA registries demonstrating baseline statin and ACEI/ARB ( online supplemental table S3 ), we anticipated up to 30% of UC patients would be taking IMT, and for reasons of observed moderate adherence to IMT in clinical care, up to 30% of IMT-assigned patients were anticipated to not take the assigned IMT. Initially, 16% of participants in the UC group were receiving IMT, while only 48% of IMT participants were adherent to the strategy. Use of IMT declined over time in both arms. A sensitivity analysis of contamination using a weighted Cox proportional hazards regression model (n=2176 with complete baseline covariates stratified by site) provided estimated HR for IMT versus UC of 0.74 95% CI (0.352 to 1.558), p=0.43 ( Figure 3 ).

The anticipated MACE rate used registries of suspected ANOCA/INOCA cohorts ( online supplemental table S4 ). Enrolling only ~60% of planned, combined with the relatively lower than anticipated MACE rate (16% at 5 years vs anticipated 25% at 3 years), resulted in limited power to test MACE reduction ( online supplemental table S4 ). The design estimated effect size of 20% MACE reduction related to randomised trials of statins, LDL-C reduction and ACEI/ARB BP reduction. 812 , 14 Accordingly, LDL-C and BP as intermediate predictors of MACE were tracked. During the trial, the difference in IMT and UC ACE/ARB medications was insufficient to result in significant reductions in BP between groups; however, there was a lower LDL-C in the IMT versus UC group (time averaged difference of 7.6 (1.5 SE) mg/dL, p<0.0001) and no detectable difference in BP between groups ( online supplemental figure S4 ).
sections.discussion:
Defining treatment strategies that improve CV health in women is a research priority. The WARRIOR primary outcome yielded a neutral result, with no benefit from proven strategies effective for MACE reduction in at-risk IHD populations. The overall MACE rate was 17% during 5 years’ follow-up, and hospitalisation for angina was the cause of most (83%) of these events.

Based on the results of this trial, intensive medical therapy was not effective in lowering MACE in women with suspected ANOCA/INOCA, although limited power precludes concluding that it may not be helpful. Because the impact of ACEi/statins/aspirin was not substantially different between groups, concluding that IMT is ineffective is not factually correct. Considering clinical translation, the WARRIOR neutral result should not be considered a negative trial and be considered an opportunity to better understand contemporary clinical practice in this suspected ANOCA/INOCA population, and define future studies to address the symptom burden, morbidity and risk.

Of note, the MACE in this female population were largely driven by repeated episodes of hospital care for anginal chest pain which accrued progressively over 5 years. This result highlights the longer-term morbidity associated with suspected ANOCA/INOCA in women. Chronic angina and unstable symptoms leading to episodes of healthcare will impact on activities of daily living leading to missed work days 17 and impairment in social and family functions. 18

The WARRIOR trial in women with suspected ANOCA/INOCA documents the high burden of recurrent hospitalisation for angina during 5-year follow-up. Of note, this level of morbidity has not changed since initial reports. The trial extends prior, relatively small suspected ANOCA/INOCA intervention cohorts using intermediate outcomes such as angina, coronary flow reserve and myocardial perfusion. 819 , 25 A foundational pharmacologic probe trial conducted by the WISE investigators in 78 women with suspected ANOCA/INOCA, randomised and double blinded to maximally tolerated the ACEI quinapril versus placebo over 16 weeks, demonstrated an almost 20 point angina improvement (SAQ angina frequency score 61 to 82, p=0.037) combined with a trend for SBP reduction (126±15 to 120±16 mmHg, p=0.38) and improved coronary flow reserve. 26 Conversely, a smaller trial with ramipril, which did not impact BP, did not improve angina or coronary flow reserve in coronary microvascular dysfunction patients. 26

Lessons to be learnt from WARRIOR should inform the design of future clinical trials. Since evidence of ischaemia by invasive or non-invasive tests was not collected at baseline, there is a diagnostic gap on vasomotor endotypes. Participants were not stratified by endotype, and nor is this information currently available to help interpret the results of the trial. Future study can also learn from contemporary studies in the ANOCA/INOCA population which have included endotype-guided intervention on QoL and other intermediate outcomes. 7 27 28 Also, the inclusion of women qualified by CCTA may have lowered the MACE rate as well as the angina burden. 29 While prior registries used to estimate the angina burden in WARRIOR reported daily to weekly angina frequency and mean SAQ scores of 55–60 ( online supplemental table S2 ), 30 the mean WARRIOR baseline SAQ score of 75 is consistent with only mild angina (once per month), which would be difficult to improve. 31 This information from the WARRIOR and other contemporary trials 32 such as iCorMicA ( NCT04674449 ), which is a pragmatic, multicentre, international clinical trial of stratified medicine in angina and all participants undergo invasive coronary function testing at baseline, should be useful to inform the design of future ANOCA/INOCA clinical trials. Specifically, trial design strengths such as the increasingly recognised angina population with poor QoL will require moderate sample sizes and placebo-controlled designs due to the subjective outcomes, while outcome trials of angina hospitalisation and MACE will require large sample sizes and targeted at-risk populations 33 using site cluster designs ( table 3 ).

ANOCA, angina with no obstructive coronary artery disease; CMD, coronary microvascular dysfunction; INOCA, ischaemia with no obstructive coronary artery disease; QoL, quality of life; RCT, randomised controlled trial; SAQ, Seattle Angina Questionnaire.

In this open-label, pragmatic trial, several limitations are relevant. The lower than anticipated MACE rate, in part relating to the pandemic, resulted in limited power. There was lower than anticipated IMT adherence and use of statin, ACEI/ARB and aspirin occurred progressively in the UC group. LDL and BP were relatively well controlled at baseline in both groups and symptom burden was relatively low. The COVID-19 pandemic limited enrolment. Specific to COVID impact, admissions for acute coronary syndrome declined by up to 48% 34 while CV mortality increased significantly in the early months of the pandemic. 35 Finally, future clinical trials in ANOCA/INOCA should include men and more non-Caucasians to be generalisable.
